title: Purpose and long life
hook: people with a sense of purpose tended to live longer in a large study

segments.voice: Yesterday: two hours in nature, a line that showed up in a big survey. Your line was two hours a week. Did the first piece make it onto your calendar? Day one thousand three hundred forty-three.

Somewhere on a long questionnaire sits a quiet question. Roughly: do you have a sense of direction in your life, or do you mostly drift? Thousands of American adults answered questions like that, along with many others about their health and their days. Then the researchers did something patient. They waited. Years later, they went back to the records and checked who was still alive. Today's study comes out of that waiting, and what it says about purpose is worth hearing slowly, without rounding it up.
screen: `DIRECTION, OR DRIFT?` → `THOUSANDS ANSWERED.` → `THEN THE RESEARCHERS WAITED.`

segments.voice: First, the finding. The psychologists Patrick Hill and Nicholas Turiano reported in the journal Psychological Science that people with a stronger sense of purpose were less likely to die over the years of the study, even after accounting for other factors they had measured. Second, the surprise. The link didn't belong only to older people. It showed up among younger adults, the middle-aged and older adults alike. Purpose wasn't just a question for retirement. Third, the caution. Nobody was assigned a purpose in this study. People simply reported how they felt about their lives. Purpose can travel with other things, like good health, steady work or close friends, and a questionnaire can't fully separate them. So the study supports a link. It doesn't promise that finding a purpose will add years to anyone's life. Fourth, what purpose looks like up close. The Roman emperor Marcus Aurelius wrote his notebooks to himself, and one entry starts with a very ordinary struggle: not wanting to get out of bed. His answer, in George Long's translation: "I am rising to the work of a human being." Not a grand mission. Not a master plan. Just the ordinary work of being a person, done on purpose. That may be a useful way to read the study, too. The purpose people reported wasn't measured in size. It was a sense of direction. Purpose.
screen: `PURPOSE LINKED TO LONGER LIFE.` · `YOUNG, MIDDLE-AGED AND OLDER ALIKE.` · `A LINK, NOT A PROMISE.` · then, large: `THE WORK OF A HUMAN BEING.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: one line of purpose. Sit comfortably and let the breath slow. Then let a sentence begin: I'm here to… and see what finishes it. Keep it small enough to be true this week. To raise a kind kid. To make good bread. To tell the truth at work. To look after my mother. If several lines come, pick the one that feels most like yours. If nothing comes, sit with the question itself; that counts. The bell holds the time.
Purpose and long life. In one long study, a sense of direction went with a longer life. A link worth knowing, not a promise. Today's word.
Your line: purpose. Today, write your one line down, on paper or in your phone, and read it once before you sleep. Day one thousand three hundred forty-three.

howItsDone: Some contemplative and philosophical traditions ask people to name what they live for; some people write a single sentence of purpose and return to it each morning or evening.

fork.setup: you're Marcus Aurelius. it's morning, and you don't want to get up. what do you tell yourself?
options: "I am rising to the work of a human being."
"I'll get up when I feel like it."
fork.reveal: he reminds himself what he's for: the ordinary work of being a person. not a grand mission, just a direction.

trapdoor: what you thought: purpose means a big life mission.
what it means: in one long study, people who reported a sense of direction were less likely to die over the years that followed.
what a scholar hears: an observational cohort study. the link held across ages and after adjusting for other measured factors, but purpose wasn't assigned, so it can't prove cause.

sources.ref: Hill, P. L., and Turiano, N. A., "Purpose in life as a predictor of mortality across adulthood," Psychological Science (2014)

notes: Check the study summary against Hill and Turiano (2014): 'thousands of American adults' (the MIDUS sample), follow-up over years, lower mortality with higher purpose after adjusting for other measured factors, and that the effect did not differ by age.
The hook's questionnaire item is a plain-language paraphrase, not the scale's wording.
Confirm the Long 1862 wording of Meditations 5.1: 'I am rising to the work of a human being.'
Marcus wrote the Meditations as private notes to himself; that framing is standard but a reviewer may wish to confirm the wording.
